title: Twin Lakes well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Around Twin Lakes, most wells are under 100 ft with a 29 ft median depth and about 17 gpm yield. Here’s what that means for cost and risk.
h1: Water wells around Twin Lakes, Adams County
intro_html:
In the Twin Lakes area of Adams County you’re on the plains over the Denver Basin, with a lot of relatively shallow wells and a very heavy mix of monitoring holes. That makes the maps look crowded, but only a fraction are household or irrigation wells. The numbers here are from Colorado Division of Water Resources permits within about five miles of Twin Lakes.

I’ll walk through how deep wells actually run here, how much water they tend to make, what drilling costs look like in this part of the Denver metro fringe, and a few risks to check before you close on a property or design a new build.

sections.heading: Shallow wells on the Twin Lakes flats
sections.html:
Around Twin Lakes, wells are generally shallow by Colorado standards. The median total depth is about 29 feet, and the middle half run 20–40 feet. About 90% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, and only 3% go deeper than 300 feet, even though the deepest on record reaches 1,751 feet.

Those few very deep holes tell you the Denver Basin can be drilled much deeper if needed, but most local groundwater is tapped in shallow alluvium or upper bedrock. For a driller bidding your job, that 20–40 foot middle range usually means a short drilling window and less steel casing than in mountain areas, but they still have to be ready in case your spot lines up with one of the deeper bedrock completions.

sections.heading: How much water Twin Lakes wells produce
sections.html:
Yield numbers here are generally strong. Of the wells that report a test, the median pump yield is 17 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10 and 60 gpm. About 62% report 15 gpm or more, while only 5% fall under 1 gpm and another 5% sit in the 1–5 gpm band.

For a single house on an exempt domestic well, anything above about 2–3 gpm is usually workable with storage. Around Twin Lakes, the odds based on nearby permits favor a comfortable supply for normal household use and small outside demand. Still, you do see a minority of low producers, so I’d never skip a proper yield test on an existing well before you buy.

sections.heading: Water table and long-term trend around Twin Lakes
sections.html:
Static water levels here are quite shallow. The median depth to water is about 10 feet, and the middle half of measurements fall between 7 and 20 feet below ground. That’s part of why so many wells are less than 100 feet total depth.

The long-term record actually shows water levels getting shallower, at least where they’ve been monitored. Median static level was around 24 feet in the 1960s, about 11 feet in the 2010s, and roughly 8 feet in the 2020s. That suggests no obvious regional decline in the shallow zones around Twin Lakes, Sherrelwood, Welby, and the nearby North Washington and Berkley areas. On a building site, that shallow water table makes proper sealing, surface drainage, and septic placement even more important.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and how use has changed
sections.html:
This area has a long drilling history. There are 11,003 permits in the records within about five miles, with 5,371 shown as constructed and 6,242 listing a total depth. Drilling picked up in the 1980s with 457 permits, then jumped sharply: 1,947 in the 1990s and 1,787 in the 2000s. Activity has stayed high with 2,708 permits in the 2010s and 1,034 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025.

Most wells are tied to monitoring and environmental work, not homes. About 65% are monitoring wells, 14% domestic/household, and about 3% irrigation. All are associated with Denver Basin aquifers, often completed in alluvial or unnamed fractured-bedrock zones. Authorized (Pe, Pg) shows up on 3,712 wells, with Layne, Christensen Co. and Ground Exploration Llc also active locally.

sections.heading: What a new Twin Lakes well is likely to cost
sections.html:
Here you’re over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, which normally runs in the $50–$70 per foot drilling range. With a median depth around 29 feet, the bored hole itself typically pencils out to roughly $1,400–$2,000. That’s just the drilling portion.

By the time you add steel or PVC casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a complete, ready-to-use well around Twin Lakes commonly lands in the $7,400–$14,000 range. Costs can climb if your location requires going well beyond that 20–40 foot middle-depth band, or if access, utilities, or water-quality treatment are more complex than average.

sections.heading: Environmental and well risks to pay attention to
sections.html:
This part of Adams County has heavy environmental activity in the records. Within about 10 miles there are 690 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 184 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and one historic mine feature. That lines up with the large number of monitoring wells in the area.

From a buyer’s standpoint, that doesn’t automatically mean your Twin Lakes well is unsafe, but it does mean water quality deserves real attention. Plan on thorough lab testing for PFAS and other contaminants, especially on shallow wells with static levels around 7–20 feet. Also watch your septic design and setbacks so you don’t create your own contamination problems in a high-water-table area.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Twin Lakes well lot
sections.html:
With shallow, high-yield wells common around Twin Lakes and neighboring places like Federal Heights and Shaw Heights, the basics look favorable for household supply. The flip side is a very busy environmental and monitoring footprint, plus a shallow water table that affects foundations and septic layout.

For an existing home, pull the DWR well permit, confirm the reported depth and yield, and get updated lab testing. For vacant land, talk with a local driller about nearby wells in that same section, not just the overall median of 29 feet and 17 gpm. Factor the $7,400–$14,000 well budget into your build numbers and coordinate driveway, utilities, and septic so you’re not re-digging later.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Twin Lakes, Colorado?
faq.a: In the Twin Lakes area of Adams County, most wells are quite shallow. The median total depth is about 29 feet, and the middle half fall between 20 and 40 feet. Roughly 90% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. There are a few very deep completions, including one down to 1,751 feet, but those are the exception rather than the rule here.

faq.q: How much water do Twin Lakes wells typically produce?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally strong. The median test yield is about 17 gallons per minute, with the middle half running 10–60 gpm. Around 62% of wells with data produce 15 gpm or more, while about 5% are under 1 gpm and another 5% sit between 1 and 5 gpm. For a normal home on an exempt domestic well, those numbers usually mean a comfortable supply when the system is designed correctly.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping near Twin Lakes?
faq.a: Available data do not show a clear regional drop in the shallow groundwater. Median static water level was around 24 feet below ground in the 1960s, about 11 feet in the 2010s, and roughly 8 feet in the 2020s. Most current static levels fall in the 7–20 foot range. That said, trends can vary over short distances, so always review the specific well log for the property you’re considering.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Twin Lakes, Adams County?
faq.a: In this part of the Denver Basin, drilling typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. With a median depth of roughly 29 feet, the drilled hole alone often costs around $1,400–$2,000. Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a complete domestic well around Twin Lakes commonly falls in the $7,400–$14,000 range, depending on site specifics.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink around Twin Lakes, Colorado?
faq.a: There are many environmental activities nearby, with 690 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 184 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That’s why so many wells here are classified as monitoring wells. Domestic wells can still provide safe water, but you should budget for comprehensive lab testing of any well you plan to drink from, and consider periodic retesting over time.
